D. ADJUDICATORY DUE PROCESS
The Constitution guarantees that no person shah, be deprived of life, 
hherty, or property, without due process of law.” This language, included 
in the Fifth AmendTnent and apphed to the states in the Fourteenth 
Amendment, may result in a requirement that the government engage in 
some kind of adjudication. The legislature may fulfill this constitutional 
necessity via statutory procedural requirements. But if the relevant 
statutes do not estabhsh the procedure—or do so inadequately—the 
Constitution will address the deficit. Across both state and. federal 
governments, courts and agencies thus face questions about the situations 
that call for adjudication under the Constitution, and the types of 
procedures that agencies might use to fulfill these constitutiona 
obligations when they arise.
1. TIMING AND ELEMENTS OF A 
DUE PROCESS HEARING
In a celebrated article, the late Judge Henry Friendly identified eleven 
features that might in a particular case be regarded as essential to a fair 
hearing:
1. 
An unbiased tribunal;
2. 
Notice of the proposed action and the grounds asserted for it,
3. 
An opportunity to present reasons why the proposed action 
should not be taken;
4. 
The right to call witnesses;
5. 
The right to know the evidence against oneself;
6. 
The right to have a decision based exclusively on the evidence 
presented;
7. 
The right to counsel;
